description: Ottawa Hardware Challenge creating a Mars rover to deploy solar panels and withstand a sand storm.
summary: We built an autonomous rover that protects its own solar panels from dust storms. The rover waits inside a closed lander, detects the door opening with an infrared sensor and four light sensors, drives itself out onto the surface, and unfolds miura-fold solar panels. It then folds shut during a sandstorm, and re-deploys clean solar panels after it notices a safe environment. Our project shows that a small, low-cost rover with simple sensors can make that decision on its own, with no commands from Earth, using a fold that packs large panels into a small space for launch.
details:
What it does. Space Rover Origami is an autonomous rover that drives out of a lander, unfolds Miura-fold solar panels, and protects them from dust storms. It runs with no remote control from the moment the lander door opens.

How it works. The rover waits in the lander until its infrared sensor and light sensors detect the door opening, then drives out onto the surface. Two servos, one at each end of the panels and rotating in sync, pull the Miura fold open. Two light sensors, one at the front and one at the back, record the light level as a baseline. When both sensors see the light drop, the rover folds the panels shut and holds still through the storm. When the light returns, it reopens the panels and drives back and forth three times to shake off the remaining sand.

Hardware and software. STM32 Blue Pill microcontroller, TB6612FNG motor driver, two DC gear motors, two servos, two photoresistors, one infrared sensor, and a 4 AA battery pack. The code is C++ written in the Arduino IDE with the STM32duino core.

Benefits and impact. The Miura fold packs a large panel area into a small space for launch and opens in a single motion. Closing the panels during storms keeps dust off the cells, and the rover decides this on its own, which matters when signals from Earth are delayed.

Creativity. We paired an origami fold with a storm detector that needs no camera or weather data, only two light sensors compared against the rover’s own baseline, and added a shake-off step to clear sand after the storm.

What we considered. A baseline instead of a fixed threshold, so it works in any lighting; requiring both sensors to agree, so a single shadow does not trigger a retract; and separate power rails, so the motors and servos cannot reset the controller.
